phy_ocra.13.0.summary: When a wave meets a boundary between two materials it can be **reflected**, **refracted**, **transmitted** or **absorbed**, and what happens depends on the materials and on the wavelength of the wave. Refraction is the change of direction that happens because a wave changes **speed** as it crosses into a new material; the frequency stays the same, so the wavelength changes as well. At Higher tier you must explain refraction using **wavefronts**: one end of a wavefront reaches the new material first and slows down (or speeds up) before the rest, so the wavefront swings round and changes direction.

core.h: Four things that can happen at a boundary
core.p: When any wave (light, other EM waves, sound or water waves) reaches the boundary between two materials, its energy can be shared between several effects. Usually more than one happens at once, e.g. a window reflects a little light, transmits most of it and absorbs a small amount.
bullets: **Reflection**: the wave bounces back from the boundary into the first material.
**Refraction**: the wave changes direction as it crosses the boundary because its speed changes.
**Transmission**: the wave passes through the material and carries on.
**Absorption**: the energy of the wave is transferred to the material, usually increasing its internal energy (it warms up).
What happens depends on the **wavelength** of the wave and the **substance**.

head: Effect
What happens to the wave
Everyday example
rows: Bounces back, same speed, same wavelength
Image in a mirror, echo of sound
Changes speed and (usually) direction on entering a new material

callouts.p: Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength.

core.p: The same material can behave very differently for different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. This is why each type of EM wave has its own uses.
bullets: Glass **transmits** visible light but **absorbs** much ultraviolet and some infrared.
The atmosphere **transmits** visible light, radio waves and microwaves, but the ozone layer **absorbs** much of the Sun's ultraviolet.
Water **absorbs** microwaves of certain wavelengths strongly (used in microwave ovens).
Soft tissue **transmits** X-rays but bone **absorbs** them.
Metal **reflects** radio waves and microwaves (used in radar and microwave oven walls).
Some radio waves are **reflected** by the ionosphere while microwaves are **transmitted** through it.
Coloured filters transmit some wavelengths of visible light and absorb the rest.

callouts.p: If asked why a wave suits a job, name the interaction: 'transmitted by the atmosphere', 'absorbed by water', 'reflected by metal'.

core.h: Reflection and the law of reflection
core.p: For reflection from a smooth surface, the angles are always measured from the **normal**, a construction line drawn at 90 degrees to the surface where the ray hits it.
bullets: **Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.**
The incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane.
The reflected wave has the **same speed, frequency and wavelength** as the incident wave, because it stays in the same material.
**Specular reflection**: from a smooth surface, parallel rays stay parallel, so a clear image forms (mirror).
**Diffuse reflection**: from a rough surface, the normals point in different directions, so rays scatter and no clear image forms (paper).
Each individual ray in diffuse reflection still obeys the law of reflection.

callouts.p: A line drawn at right angles (90 degrees) to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.
Angles of incidence, reflection and refraction are measured from the normal, never from the surface.

core.p: Refraction is the **change in direction** of a wave when it passes from one material into another, caused by a **change in speed**. Light travels fastest in a vacuum (and almost as fast in air), slower in water and slower still in glass.
bullets: Wave **slows down** (e.g. air into glass): it bends **towards the normal**.
Wave **speeds up** (e.g. glass into air): it bends **away from the normal**.
If the wave hits the boundary **along the normal** (angle of incidence 0), it changes speed but **does not change direction**.
A material in which light travels more slowly is described as **optically denser**.
The bigger the change in speed, the more the wave bends.

callouts.p: The change in direction of a wave as it crosses a boundary between two materials, because its speed changes.

callouts.t: FAST to SLOW: towards the normal
callouts.p: Slowing down bends the ray towards the normal; speeding up bends it away from the normal.

core.h: Speed, frequency and wavelength during refraction
core.p: The wave equation **wave speed = frequency x wavelength** (v = f x lambda) applies in every material. When a wave crosses a boundary its **frequency does not change**, because the source sets the frequency and the waves cannot pile up or disappear at the boundary.
bullets: Frequency stays **constant**.
If speed **decreases**, wavelength **decreases** in proportion (waves bunch up).
If speed **increases**, wavelength **increases**.
Rearranged: lambda = v / f, so with f fixed, lambda is proportional to v.
Units: v in m/s, f in Hz, lambda in m.

callouts.p: A very common error is saying the frequency changes. Only speed and wavelength change on refraction.

core.p: A **wavefront** is a line joining points on a wave that are in step, such as all the crests. Rays are always at right angles to wavefronts. Refraction can be explained by what happens to different parts of the same wavefront.
bullets: A wavefront approaches the boundary **at an angle**, so one end reaches the new material first.
That end **slows down** while the rest of the wavefront is still moving at the faster speed in the first material.
The slower end travels a shorter distance in the same time, so the wavefront **swings round (pivots)**.
This changes the direction the wave travels: it bends **towards the normal**.
Wavefronts are **closer together** in the slower material because the wavelength is shorter.
If the wavefront hits the boundary **parallel** to it (ray along the normal), every part slows at the same moment, so the direction does not change.

callouts.p: Use: 'one side of the wavefront enters the glass first', 'slows down', 'the other side is still travelling faster', 'so the wavefront changes direction', 'wavelength decreases, frequency stays the same'.

core.p: Refraction is a property of **all** waves, not just light.
bullets: **Water waves** slow down when they move from deep to shallow water, so they bend and their wavelength decreases; this is why waves line up parallel to a beach.
**Sound waves** change speed in air at different temperatures, so sound can bend.
Sound travels **faster** in solids and liquids than in gases, the opposite of light.
A ripple tank is used to show refraction of water waves over a shallow region made by a glass plate.

callouts.p: Over shallow water the waves slow down and the wavefronts become closer together (shorter wavelength), with frequency unchanged.

core.h: Absorption and transmission in more detail
core.p: Whether a wave is absorbed or transmitted depends on whether the wave's frequency matches ways that the particles of the material can take in energy.
bullets: **Transparent** materials transmit light with little absorption or scattering.
**Translucent** materials transmit light but scatter it, so images are not clear.
**Opaque** materials do not transmit light; they absorb or reflect it.
Absorbed energy usually increases the **thermal energy store** of the material.
Dark, matt surfaces are good absorbers of visible light and infrared; light, shiny surfaces are good reflectors.
The amount absorbed also depends on the **thickness** of the material.

callouts.p: When a wave passes through a material rather than being reflected or absorbed.

core.h: Partial reflection and total internal reflection
core.p: At most boundaries some of the wave is reflected and some refracted. When light travels from a denser material (glass) to a less dense one (air), it bends away from the normal; at a large enough angle no light can leave.
bullets: At a glass to air boundary there is always a weak reflected ray as well as the refracted ray.
As the angle of incidence increases, the refracted ray bends closer to the surface.
At the **critical angle** the refracted ray travels along the boundary.
Above the critical angle, all the light is reflected: **total internal reflection**.
Total internal reflection is used in **optical fibres**.

core.h: Investigating refraction with a glass block
core.p: A common practical uses a ray box and a rectangular glass block to measure angles of incidence and refraction.
bullets: Draw round the block on paper, then shine a narrow ray of light into one side at an angle.
Mark the incident and emerging rays with crosses, remove the block and join the points through the block.
Draw the **normal** at the point of entry with a protractor and measure angle of incidence i and angle of refraction r.
Repeat for several values of i; r is always smaller than i for air into glass.
The emerging ray is **parallel** to the incident ray for a rectangular block (it is displaced sideways).
Use a darkened room and a **narrow** ray to reduce uncertainty in angles.

callouts.p: A thin, sharp ray and marking points far apart along each ray reduce the uncertainty in drawing lines and measuring angles.

analogy.p: Picture a row of marchers walking at an angle from a tarmac path onto a muddy field. The marchers at one end reach the mud first and slow down, while those still on tarmac keep their speed. The row swings round and the band heads off in a new direction, closer to the normal. Each marcher keeps the same step rate (frequency) but takes shorter steps (wavelength). It breaks down because real waves are not made of separate people, part of the wave can also be reflected, and light waves need no medium at all.

mistakes.r: Frequency is unchanged; speed and wavelength decrease.

mistakes.r: All angles are measured from the normal.

mistakes.r: Light slows down entering glass so bends towards the normal.

mistakes.r: Its speed and wavelength still change; only its direction stays the same.

exam.q: State the law of reflection.
model: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
exam.tip: Write it as a full statement.

exam.q: What is meant by the normal?
model: A line at 90 degrees (perpendicular) to the surface at the point where the ray meets it.
exam.tip: Include the point of incidence.

exam.q: Light travels from air into water. State what happens to its speed, frequency and wavelength.
model: Speed decreases.
Frequency stays the same.
Wavelength decreases.
exam.tip: Three separate statements.

exam.q: Explain why a ray of light bends towards the normal when it enters a glass block at an angle.
model: Light slows down in glass.
The change in speed causes a change in direction towards the normal.
exam.tip: Link speed change to direction.

exam.q: A light wave has frequency 5.0 x 10^14 Hz and travels at 2.0 x 10^8 m/s in glass. Calculate its wavelength in glass.
model: lambda = v / f
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: Give one example of an electromagnetic wave that is transmitted by one substance but absorbed by another.
model: e.g. X-rays transmitted by soft tissue / absorbed by bone.
or visible light transmitted by glass, UV absorbed by glass; microwaves absorbed by water but transmitted by glass.
exam.tip: Name the wave and both substances.

exam.q: Explain the difference between specular and diffuse reflection.
model: Specular: reflection from a smooth surface, parallel rays stay parallel / clear image.
Diffuse: reflection from a rough surface, rays scattered in different directions / no clear image.
exam.tip: Mention smooth versus rough.

exam.q: A ray of light hits a glass block along the normal. Describe what happens to it.
model: It does not change direction.
It slows down / its wavelength decreases.
exam.tip: Direction unchanged, speed still changes.

exam.q: Use the idea of wavefronts to explain why light changes direction when it passes from air into glass at an angle.
model: Wavefronts meet the boundary at an angle.
One side of each wavefront enters the glass first.
That side slows down.
The rest of the wavefront is still in air, travelling faster.
So the wavefront changes direction / pivots, bending towards the normal.
Wavelength becomes shorter in glass; frequency stays the same.
exam.tip: Level 3 needs a full sequence plus wavelength/frequency comment; a labelled wavefront sketch helps.

exam.q: Water waves travel from deep water to shallow water. Their speed falls from 0.30 m/s to 0.20 m/s and their frequency is 2.0 Hz. Calculate the change in wavelength.
model: Deep: lambda = 0.30 / 2.0 = 0.15 m.
Shallow: lambda = 0.20 / 2.0 = 0.10 m.
Change = decrease of 0.05 m.
exam.tip: Frequency is the same in both.

worked.q: Light of wavelength 6.0 x 10^-7 m in air (speed 3.0 x 10^8 m/s) enters glass where its speed is 2.0 x 10^8 m/s. Find the frequency and the wavelength in glass.
steps: Frequency f = v / lambda = 3.0 x 10^8 / 6.0 x 10^-7 = 5.0 x 10^14 Hz.
Frequency is unchanged in glass, so f = 5.0 x 10^14 Hz.
Wavelength in glass = v / f = 2.0 x 10^8 / 5.0 x 10^14 = 4.0 x 10^-7 m.
Check: speed fell to two thirds, so wavelength fell to two thirds.
worked.ans: f = 5.0 x 10^14 Hz in both; wavelength in glass = 4.0 x 10^-7 m.

worked.q: A student shines a ray into a rectangular glass block at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees and measures an angle of refraction of 25 degrees. She says the emerging ray will be parallel to the incident ray. Explain why.
steps: At the first surface light slows down and bends towards the normal (40 to 25 degrees).
The two faces of the block are parallel, so at the second face the angle of incidence inside the glass is again 25 degrees.
Light speeds up leaving the glass and bends away from the normal back to 40 degrees.
So the emerging ray leaves at the same angle as it entered, displaced sideways.
worked.ans: The ray is refracted by equal and opposite amounts at two parallel faces, so it emerges parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways.

phy_ocra.13.1.summary: Lenses work by **refraction**: light changes speed and direction as it enters and leaves the glass, and the curved surfaces make different rays bend by different amounts. A **convex (converging)** lens brings parallel rays together at a **principal focus**, while a **concave (diverging)** lens spreads parallel rays out so they appear to come from a principal focus on the same side as the light. Ray diagrams use a few standard rays to find where an image forms and whether it is **real or virtual**, **upright or inverted**, and **magnified or diminished**. In PAG P4 you investigate lenses, for example measuring the focal length of a convex lens.

core.p: A lens is a shaped piece of transparent material such as glass or plastic. Light slows down as it enters the lens and speeds up as it leaves, so it **refracts** at both surfaces. Because the surfaces are curved, rays hitting different parts of the lens meet the surface at different angles and bend by different amounts.
bullets: Rays through the **thin centre** of a lens pass straight through (the two surfaces are almost parallel there).
Rays further from the centre meet the surface at a steeper angle, so they are bent more.
In a convex lens the outer rays bend **towards** the axis; in a concave lens they bend **away** from it.
On ray diagrams we draw all the bending happening at the centre line of the lens to keep things simple.

callouts.p: Lenses form images by refraction, not reflection.

core.p: Every ray diagram uses the same set of terms, and mark schemes expect them exactly.
bullets: **Principal axis**: the line through the centre of the lens at right angles to it.
**Principal focus (focal point, F)**: for a convex lens, the point where rays parallel to the axis **meet** after passing through; for a concave lens, the point from which they **appear to come**.
**Focal length (f)**: the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
There is a principal focus on **each side** of a lens, the same distance away.
A **more curved** (fatter) lens refracts light more, so it has a **shorter focal length** and is more powerful.

callouts.p: The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

core.p: A convex lens is thicker in the middle than at the edges. It **converges** light: parallel rays are refracted so they all pass through the principal focus on the far side.
bullets: Parallel rays meet at a **real** focus: light actually passes through it, so a screen placed there would show a bright spot.
The ray diagram symbol is a vertical line with **outward pointing arrowheads** at each end.
Uses: magnifying glasses, cameras, projectors, the lens in the eye, correcting long sight.
The image formed depends on how far the object is from the lens.

fig.cap: A convex (converging) lens refracts rays parallel to the principal axis so that they all pass through the principal focus F. The distance from the lens centre to F is the focal length.

core.p: A concave lens is thinner in the middle than at the edges. It **diverges** light: parallel rays spread out after the lens as if they had come from the principal focus on the **same side** as the incoming light.
bullets: The focus is **virtual**: the rays do not really pass through it; they only appear to come from it.
On a diagram, extend the diverging rays **backwards with dashed lines** to show they meet at F.
The ray diagram symbol is a vertical line with **inward pointing arrowheads** (like a V at each end).
A concave lens always forms a **virtual, upright, diminished** image, on the same side as the object.
Uses: correcting **short sight**, door peepholes, some telescopes and cameras in combination with convex lenses.

callouts.p: Construction lines showing where rays appear to come from must be dashed; real rays are solid with arrows.

core.p: The spec asks you to show the **similarity and difference** in how the two lenses refract light.
bullets: Similarity: both refract light at both surfaces because light changes speed in glass.
Similarity: a ray through the centre passes straight through both types.
Difference: convex brings rays together (converges), concave spreads them apart (diverges).
Difference: convex has a real focus, concave has a virtual focus.

Convex (converging)
Concave (diverging)

core.p: To draw a ray diagram, start from the **top of the object** and draw at least **two** of these rays. Where the rays (or their dashed extensions) cross is the top of the image.
bullets: **Ray 1**: parallel to the principal axis, then refracted **through F** on the far side (convex), or so that it **appears to come from F** on the near side (concave).
**Ray 2**: through the **centre** of the lens, carrying on **undeviated** (straight).
**Ray 3** (convex): through F on the near side, then emerges **parallel** to the axis.
**Ray 3** (concave): heading towards F on the far side, then emerges parallel to the axis.
Draw rays with a **ruler** and arrows showing direction.
The object is usually drawn as an upright arrow standing on the principal axis.

callouts.p: Rays 1 and 2 are the easiest and are enough to locate the image. Use ray 3 as a check.

core.p: Exam questions usually ask you to describe the image using three pairs of words.
bullets: **Real** (rays actually meet, can be shown on a screen) or **virtual** (rays only appear to come from it, cannot be put on a screen).
**Upright** (same way up as the object) or **inverted** (upside down).
**Magnified** (bigger than the object), **same size**, or **diminished** (smaller).
Also state the **position**, e.g. 'between F and 2F on the other side of the lens'.
**Magnification = image height / object height** (no units).

callouts.p: An image formed where light rays actually meet; it can be projected onto a screen.
An image from which light rays only appear to come; it cannot be projected onto a screen.

core.p: When the object is **further than 2F** from a convex lens, the image is formed on the other side between F and 2F.
bullets: Image is **real, inverted and diminished**.
This is how a **camera** and the **eye** form an image on the sensor or retina.
Object exactly at 2F: image at 2F, real, inverted, **same size**.
Object between F and 2F: image beyond 2F, real, inverted, **magnified** (used in a **projector**).
Object very far away: rays arrive parallel and the image forms at F (used to find focal length).
Object at F: rays emerge parallel and **no image** is formed.

core.h: Convex lens as a magnifying glass
core.p: When the object is **closer to the lens than F**, the rays leaving the lens diverge and never meet. Your eye traces them back to where they appear to come from, which is a **virtual** image.
bullets: Image is **virtual, upright and magnified**, on the **same side** as the object.
Extend the emerging rays backwards with **dashed lines** until they meet.
The image is further from the lens than the object.
The image cannot be put on a screen; you see it by looking through the lens.

callouts.p: Object inside F of a convex lens gives a virtual, upright, magnified image.

core.p: For a concave lens, wherever the object is, the image is on the same side as the object, between F and the lens.
bullets: Ray 1: from the top of the object parallel to the axis; after the lens it diverges as if it came from F on the object side (draw a dashed line back to F).
Ray 2: from the top of the object straight through the centre of the lens.
The image is where the dashed line from ray 1 crosses ray 2.
Image is always **virtual, upright and diminished**.
This is why objects look smaller through a door peephole or through glasses for short sight.

core.h: PAG P4: finding the focal length of a convex lens
core.p: A simple, quick method uses a **distant object**, whose rays arrive almost parallel, so the image forms at the principal focus.
bullets: Fix the lens in a holder and point it at a distant object such as a window or tree across the room or outside.
Move a white **screen** behind the lens until a **sharp, focused**, inverted image appears.
Measure the distance from the **centre of the lens** to the screen with a metre rule: this is the **focal length**.
Repeat several times, moving the screen away and refocusing each time, and calculate a **mean**.
Alternative: use a ray box with several parallel rays and mark where they cross.
Extension: place an illuminated object (cross-wire) at measured distances and record where a sharp image forms; observe how image size and orientation change.

callouts.p: Judging the sharpest image is the main source of uncertainty. Approach the focus from both sides and take a mean; work in a darkened room for a clearer image.
Never focus sunlight with a lens onto skin or paper, and never look at the Sun through a lens.

core.h: Lenses in the eye and in glasses
core.p: The eye contains a convex lens that forms a real, inverted, diminished image on the retina. Glasses correct the eye when the image is not focused on the retina.
bullets: **Short sight** (myopia): distant objects focus in front of the retina; corrected with a **concave (diverging)** lens.
**Long sight** (hyperopia): near objects focus behind the retina; corrected with a **convex (converging)** lens.
A lens with a shorter focal length is more powerful and bends light more.

analogy.p: Think of light rays as cars and a lens as a road junction. A convex lens is like a set of lanes that all steer cars towards one roundabout (the focus), so they all meet there. A concave lens is like lanes that fan out from a junction, so to an observer ahead the cars all seem to have come from one point behind the junction. The car through the middle goes straight on. It breaks down because cars steer by choice, while light bends only because its speed changes at the glass surfaces, and real lenses do not focus all colours to exactly the same point.

terms.d: A lens thicker at the centre than the edges that converges parallel rays to a real focus.
A lens thinner at the centre than the edges that diverges parallel rays so they appear to come from a virtual focus.
Bringing rays of light together.
Spreading rays of light apart.
The line through the centre of a lens at right angles to the lens.
The point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet (convex) or appear to come from (concave) after refraction.
The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
An image formed where rays actually meet; can be projected on a screen.
An image from which rays only appear to come; cannot be projected on a screen.
Upside down compared with the object.
The same way up as the object.
Larger than the object.
Smaller than the object.
Image height divided by object height; it has no units.
A scale drawing using standard rays to find the position and nature of an image.
Change in direction of light at a boundary caused by a change in speed; the process by which lenses work.

mistakes.w: Lenses reflect light to form an image.
mistakes.r: Lenses refract light.

mistakes.w: Ray through the centre bends towards F.
mistakes.r: The ray through the centre of the lens passes straight through undeviated.

mistakes.w: A concave lens focuses light to a real focus.
mistakes.r: A concave lens diverges light; its focus is virtual (rays appear to come from it).

mistakes.w: Drawing the backward extensions of rays as solid lines.
mistakes.r: Virtual rays and virtual images are drawn with dashed lines.

mistakes.w: Focal length is the distance from the object to the image.
mistakes.r: Focal length is the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

mistakes.w: A magnifying glass gives a real, magnified image.
mistakes.r: With the object inside F the image is virtual, upright and magnified.

mistakes.w: A fatter lens has a longer focal length.
mistakes.r: A more curved lens refracts more, so it has a shorter focal length.

mistakes.w: Describing the image as 'big and upside down'.
mistakes.r: Use the terms real/virtual, upright/inverted, magnified/diminished.

exam.q: State the type of lens used in a magnifying glass.
model: Convex / converging lens.
exam.tip: Either name is accepted.

exam.q: Define the focal length of a lens.
model: Distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
exam.tip: Say centre of the lens.

exam.q: Describe what happens to rays of light parallel to the principal axis when they pass through a concave lens.
model: They are refracted / spread out (diverge).
They appear to come from the principal focus on the same side as the incoming light.
exam.tip: Mention 'appear to come from'.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a real image and a virtual image.
model: Real image: rays actually meet, can be shown on a screen.
Virtual image: rays only appear to come from it, cannot be shown on a screen.
exam.tip: The screen test is the easiest discriminator.

exam.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Describe the image formed.
model: Real.
Inverted.
Diminished (formed between F and 2F on the other side).
exam.tip: 30 cm is beyond 2F (20 cm).

exam.q: Draw a ray diagram to show how a convex lens forms an image of an object placed between F and the lens.
model: Ray parallel to axis refracted through F on far side.
Ray through centre undeviated.
Rays extended backwards with dashed lines to meet.
Image shown upright, magnified, on same side as object (virtual).
exam.tip: Use a ruler; put arrows on rays.

exam.q: State two similarities between the way light is refracted by convex and concave lenses.
model: Both refract light because light changes speed in the lens.
A ray through the centre passes straight through both / both have a principal focus on each side at the focal length.
exam.tip: Similarities, not differences.

exam.q: A student measures the focal length of a convex lens by focusing a distant window on a screen. Her results are 14.8 cm, 15.3 cm and 15.1 cm. Calculate the mean focal length.
exam.tip: Give the same number of decimal places as the data.

exam.q: Describe how to determine the focal length of a convex lens in the laboratory. Include how to make the result as accurate as possible.
model: Point the lens at a distant object (e.g. window) so rays arriving are parallel.
Place a screen behind the lens and move it until a sharp image is seen.
Measure the distance from the centre of the lens to the screen with a metre rule.
This distance is the focal length.
Repeat, refocusing each time, and calculate a mean.
Use a darkened room / approach focus from both sides / keep lens and screen perpendicular to the rule.
exam.tip: Level 3 needs method, measurement and accuracy improvements.

exam.q: An image is 6.0 mm tall and the object is 2.0 mm tall. Calculate the magnification.
model: magnification = image height / object height = 6.0 / 2.0
= 3 (no units)
exam.tip: Magnification has no units.

worked.q: An object 4.0 cm tall is 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 5.0 cm. Using a scale drawing (1 square = 1 cm) find the image position, height and magnification.
steps: Draw the lens and principal axis; mark F at 5 cm and 2F at 10 cm on each side.
Draw the object 4 cm tall, 15 cm to the left (beyond 2F).
Ray 1: from the top of the object parallel to the axis, then through F on the right.
Ray 2: from the top of the object straight through the centre.
Rays cross 7.5 cm to the right of the lens, 2.0 cm below the axis.
Magnification = 2.0 / 4.0 = 0.5.
worked.ans: Image 7.5 cm from the lens on the other side, 2.0 cm tall, real, inverted, diminished; magnification 0.5.

worked.q: A stamp 1.0 cm tall is held 3.0 cm from a magnifying glass of focal length 6.0 cm. A scale drawing shows the image 6.0 cm from the lens on the same side, 2.0 cm tall. Describe the image and calculate the magnification.
steps: Object is inside F (3 cm < 6 cm), so the rays diverge after the lens.
Dashed backward extensions meet on the same side as the object, so the image is virtual.
The image is the same way up, so it is upright.
Magnification = 2.0 / 1.0 = 2.
worked.ans: Virtual, upright, magnified image, 6.0 cm from the lens on the same side; magnification 2.

phy_ocra.13.2.summary: Ray diagrams are simple scale-free drawings that show the path light takes when it reflects off a surface or refracts as it crosses a boundary between two materials. For reflection, the **angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection**, both measured from the **normal**. For refraction, light bends **towards the normal** when it slows down entering a denser material such as glass, and **away from the normal** when it speeds up leaving it. OCR only asks for qualitative diagrams, so you must draw rays with a ruler, add arrows, draw the normal and bend the ray the correct way.

core.p: A **ray** is a straight line with an arrow that shows the direction energy (light) travels. A ray diagram uses a few rays to show what happens to light at a surface. OCR P5.3d asks you to **construct two-dimensional ray diagrams** for reflection and refraction; this is qualitative, so no equations such as Snell's law are needed.
bullets: Always draw rays with a **ruler and sharp pencil**.
Every ray needs an **arrow** showing the direction of travel.
Light travels in **straight lines** in one material; it only changes direction at a boundary.
The point where the ray hits the surface is the **point of incidence**.
Marks are awarded for: correct normal, correct angles, correct direction of bending and arrows.

callouts.p: A straight line with an arrow that shows the path and direction of travel of light.

core.p: Every angle in a ray diagram is measured from the **normal**, an imaginary line drawn at **90 degrees to the surface** at the point where the ray hits it. It is usually drawn as a **dashed line** so it is not confused with a ray.
bullets: Draw the normal **perpendicular** (at right angles) to the boundary at the point of incidence.
Draw it as a **dashed (broken) line** extending on both sides of the boundary.
Angles are measured between the ray and the normal, **never between the ray and the surface**.
For a curved surface the normal is along the radius, through the centre of curvature.

callouts.p: A line drawn at right angles (90 degrees) to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.
If you measure from the surface you get 90 degrees minus the correct angle and lose the mark.

core.p: When light reflects from a smooth surface such as a plane mirror, it bounces off so that the **angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection**. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the **same plane** (the flat page in a 2D diagram).
bullets: **Angle of incidence (i)**: angle between the incident ray and the normal.
**Angle of reflection (r)**: angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
**i = r** for every reflection from a smooth surface.
A ray hitting the mirror **along the normal** (i = 0) reflects straight back along itself.
The reflected ray is on the **opposite side of the normal** from the incident ray.

callouts.p: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

fig.cap: Reflection at a plane mirror. The dashed normal is at 90 degrees to the mirror; angle i (incidence) equals angle r (reflection).

core.h: How to draw a reflection ray diagram step by step
core.p: Exam questions often give you the mirror and the incident ray and ask you to complete the diagram. Follow a fixed routine so you never miss a mark.
bullets: 1. Mark the **point of incidence** where the incident ray meets the mirror.
2. Use a protractor or set square to draw the **normal at 90 degrees** to the mirror (dashed).
3. Measure the **angle of incidence** between the incident ray and the normal.
4. On the other side of the normal, measure the **same angle** and draw the reflected ray with a ruler.
5. Add **arrows** on both rays pointing away from the source.
6. Label i and r if asked.

callouts.p: Examiners usually allow plus or minus 2 degrees, so a neat protractor measurement secures the mark.

core.p: Reflection from a **smooth** surface such as a mirror is **specular**: parallel incoming rays stay parallel, so a clear image forms. Reflection from a **rough** surface such as paper is **diffuse**: each tiny part of the surface has a normal pointing a different way, so parallel rays are scattered in many directions and no image forms.
bullets: The law of reflection (i = r) is obeyed at **every point** in both cases.
In diffuse reflection the **normals point in different directions**, so the reflected rays spread out.
Diffuse reflection is why you can see a page from any angle but cannot see your face in it.
Specular reflection gives a clear image (mirrors, still water).

head: Type
Surface
What happens to parallel rays
Image?
rows: Reflected rays scattered in many directions

callouts.p: Do not write that rough surfaces break the law of reflection. Each ray still has i = r about its own local normal.

core.p: Rays from an object reflect off the mirror and enter your eye. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it traces the rays back behind the mirror to where they appear to come from. That point is the **image**.
bullets: The image is **virtual**: rays only appear to come from it, so it cannot be put on a screen.
The image is the **same distance behind** the mirror as the object is in front.
The image is the **same size** as the object and **upright**.
The image is **laterally inverted** (left and right swapped).
Extensions of reflected rays behind the mirror are drawn as **dashed lines** because no light actually travels there.

callouts.p: An image formed where rays appear to come from; it cannot be projected on a screen.

core.h: What refraction is and why it happens
core.p: **Refraction** is the change in direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary between two materials at an angle. It happens because the **speed of the wave changes**. Light travels more slowly in glass, water or Perspex than in air.
bullets: Light slows down when it enters a **more optically dense** material (air to glass).
Light speeds up when it enters a **less optically dense** material (glass to air).
If the ray meets the boundary at an angle, one side of the wavefront reaches the new material first and changes speed first, so the wave **swings round** and changes direction.
The **frequency stays the same**; the speed and wavelength change.
If the ray hits **along the normal** (at 90 degrees to the surface) it changes speed but **does not change direction**.

callouts.p: The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium into another, caused by a change in its speed.
Refraction is caused by a change in wave speed at the boundary, not by the boundary itself.

core.h: Direction of bending: towards or away from the normal
core.p: The single most important rule in refraction diagrams is which way the ray bends. Use speed to decide.
bullets: **Slows down** (air into glass or water): bends **towards the normal**, so angle of refraction is **smaller** than angle of incidence.
**Speeds up** (glass or water into air): bends **away from the normal**, so angle of refraction is **larger** than angle of incidence.
**Along the normal**: passes straight through, no bending.
The **angle of refraction** is measured between the refracted ray and the normal.

head: Boundary
Speed change
Bends
Angle of refraction compared with i

callouts.p: SLow = Lean in (towards normal). Speeds up = swings out (away from normal).

core.h: Refraction through a rectangular glass block
core.p: This is the classic diagram. A ray enters the block, bends towards the normal, travels straight across the block, then bends away from the normal as it leaves. Because the two faces are **parallel**, the **emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray** but **displaced sideways**.
bullets: Draw a normal at the **entry point** and another at the **exit point**.
At entry: air to glass, ray bends **towards** the normal.
Inside the block: ray is a **straight line** joining entry and exit points.
At exit: glass to air, ray bends **away** from the normal.
Emergent ray is **parallel to the incident ray** (same direction), shifted sideways.
A small amount of light is also **partially reflected** at each surface.

callouts.p: For a rectangular block the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray because the bending at exit exactly reverses the bending at entry.

core.h: Light leaving glass or water into air
core.p: When light travels from glass or water into air it speeds up and bends **away from the normal**. This explains why a swimming pool looks **shallower** than it really is and why a straw looks bent in a glass of water.
bullets: Rays from the bottom of the pool bend away from the normal at the surface.
Your eye traces the rays back in straight lines, so the bottom **appears higher** (shallower) than it is.
A pencil in water appears **bent at the surface** for the same reason.
The angle of refraction in air is **larger** than the angle of incidence in water.

callouts.p: For a 4 or 6 mark question, say: light from the object refracts away from the normal as it leaves the water; the brain assumes light travels in straight lines; so the image appears nearer the surface.

fig.cap: Light passing from glass into air speeds up and bends away from the normal, so the angle of refraction r is larger than the angle of incidence i.

core.p: At any boundary between two transparent materials, most light is **transmitted** (and refracted) but some is **reflected**. A full ray diagram may show a faint reflected ray obeying i = r alongside the refracted ray.
bullets: The partially reflected ray stays in the **first medium** and obeys **i = r**.
The refracted ray enters the **second medium** and bends according to the speed change.
This is why you can see a faint reflection of yourself in a shop window.
Reflection, refraction (transmission) and absorption can all happen at one boundary.

core.p: Rays are drawn at right angles to **wavefronts**. When wavefronts hit a boundary at an angle, the part that enters the slower material first slows down while the rest is still moving fast. The wavefront pivots, so the direction of the ray changes.
bullets: Wavefronts get **closer together** in the slower material because the **wavelength decreases** (v = f x wavelength, with f unchanged).
The edge entering first travels a **shorter distance** in the same time, so the wavefront turns towards the normal.
Leaving the slower material, the reverse happens and the wavefront turns away from the normal.
Analogy: a pair of wheels rolling from tarmac onto sand at an angle swings round as one wheel slows first.

callouts.p: Frequency is set by the source and does not change at a boundary; speed and wavelength change together.

core.p: Most lost marks in ray diagrams come from careless construction rather than poor understanding. Use this checklist before moving on.
bullets: Normal drawn at **90 degrees**, dashed, at **every** point where a ray meets a surface.
Arrows on **every** ray, in the direction light travels.
Reflection: angle of reflection **equal** to angle of incidence.
Refraction into denser material: ray **closer** to the normal.
Refraction out of denser material: ray **further** from the normal.
Ray inside the block is **straight**.
Emergent ray from a parallel-sided block **parallel** to the incident ray.
Rays drawn with a **ruler**; no gaps or wobbly lines.

callouts.p: Light changes direction only at the boundary. Never draw a curved ray inside the glass.

analogy.p: Imagine a line of marchers walking arm in arm from a smooth car park onto a muddy field at an angle. The marchers who reach the mud first slow down while the others are still fast, so the whole line swings round and changes direction, turning towards the normal. Walking back out onto the car park, the first marchers to leave speed up and the line swings the other way, away from the normal. If they walk straight at the mud (along the normal) everyone slows at once and the line does not turn. Where it breaks down: marchers are separate people who could choose to change direction, whereas light has no choice, and real light also partly reflects at the boundary, which the marchers do not.

terms.d: A straight line with an arrow showing the path and direction of travel of light.
A line at 90 degrees to a surface at the point where a ray meets it; angles are measured from it.
The point where the incident ray meets the surface or boundary.
The ray travelling towards a surface.
The ray that bounces back off a surface into the same medium.
The ray that has changed direction after passing into a second medium.
The ray that leaves a block or object after refracting at its far surface.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal; equal to the angle of incidence.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
The change in direction of a wave crossing a boundary between media, caused by a change in speed.
Describes a material in which light travels more slowly, such as glass or water compared with air.
Reflection from a smooth surface where parallel rays remain parallel, producing a clear image.
Reflection from a rough surface where parallel rays are scattered in many directions, so no image forms.
An image from which rays only appear to come; it cannot be formed on a screen.
A line joining points on a wave that are in step, such as all the crests; rays are at 90 degrees to wavefronts.

mistakes.w: Measuring the angle of incidence from the mirror surface.
mistakes.r: The angle of incidence is measured between the ray and the normal.

mistakes.w: Drawing the normal as a solid line or not at 90 degrees to the surface.
mistakes.r: Normal drawn dashed and perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.

mistakes.w: Light bends away from the normal when it enters glass.
mistakes.r: Light slows down entering glass so it bends towards the normal.

mistakes.w: Light bends because the glass is thicker or heavier.
mistakes.r: Light refracts because its speed changes at the boundary.

mistakes.w: A ray entering along the normal bends.
mistakes.r: A ray along the normal changes speed but does not change direction.

mistakes.w: The emergent ray from a rectangular block continues in a new direction.
mistakes.r: The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, displaced sideways.

mistakes.w: The frequency of light changes when it enters glass.
mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength decrease.

mistakes.w: Rough surfaces do not obey the law of reflection.
mistakes.r: Each ray still obeys i = r but the normals point in different directions, so the light is scattered (diffuse reflection).

mistakes.w: Forgetting arrows on rays.
mistakes.r: Every ray must have an arrow showing the direction light travels.

exam.q: State the law of reflection.
model: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from the normal).
exam.tip: Name both angles; i = r alone is usually accepted only if i and r are defined.

exam.q: What is meant by the normal in a ray diagram?
model: A line at right angles (90 degrees) to the surface at the point where the ray meets it.
exam.tip: Say 90 degrees to the surface, not to the ray.

exam.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 35 degrees. State the angle of reflection and the angle between the reflected ray and the mirror surface.
model: Angle of reflection = 35 degrees.
Angle between reflected ray and mirror = 90 - 35 = 55 degrees.
exam.tip: Watch for questions that give the angle to the surface; subtract from 90 first.

exam.q: Complete a ray diagram to show a ray of light passing from air into a glass block at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees.
model: Normal drawn at 90 degrees to the surface at the point of incidence.
Refracted ray drawn in glass bending towards the normal (angle of refraction less than 40 degrees).
exam.tip: Use a ruler and add an arrow; a curved ray loses the mark.

exam.q: Explain why light changes direction when it passes from air into water at an angle.
model: Light slows down in water.
One side of the wavefront slows first, so the wave changes direction (bends towards the normal).
exam.tip: Speed change is the key word; it is the cause of refraction.

exam.q: A ray of light strikes the surface of a glass block along the normal. Describe what happens to the ray.
model: It slows down (speed decreases).
It does not change direction / passes straight through.
exam.tip: Two separate effects, two marks: speed and direction.

exam.q: Draw and describe the path of a ray of light through a rectangular glass block, entering one face at an angle.
model: Normals drawn at entry and exit points.
Ray bends towards the normal on entering the glass.
Ray travels in a straight line through the glass.
Ray bends away from the normal on leaving; emergent ray parallel to incident ray.
exam.tip: State parallel emergent ray explicitly for the final mark.

exam.q: Explain the difference between specular and diffuse reflection.
model: Specular reflection occurs at a smooth surface.
Parallel rays are reflected parallel, producing a clear image.
Diffuse reflection occurs at a rough surface.
Normals point in different directions so rays are scattered; each ray still obeys i = r.
exam.tip: Mention the law still applies in diffuse reflection to reach the top mark.

exam.q: A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is. Explain why, using ideas about refraction.
model: Light from the bottom of the pool travels from water into air.
It speeds up and bends away from the normal at the surface.
The observer's brain assumes light travels in straight lines.
So the rays appear to come from a point higher up / the bottom appears nearer the surface.
exam.tip: A sketch with dashed extensions backwards can support your answer.

exam.q: Describe how you would use a ray box, a rectangular glass block and a protractor to investigate how light refracts at a boundary, and what you would expect to find.
model: Place the block on paper and draw round it; shine a narrow ray from the ray box at the side of the block.
Mark the incident and emergent rays with crosses, remove the block and join the points with a ruler.
Draw the normal at the entry point at 90 degrees to the surface.
Measure the angle of incidence and angle of refraction with a protractor; repeat for a range of angles of incidence.
Expect the angle of refraction to be smaller than the angle of incidence (bends towards normal) because light slows in glass.
Expect a ray along the normal to pass undeviated, and the emergent ray to be parallel to the incident ray; do in a darkened room for a clear ray.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need method, measurement and expected results in a logical order.

worked.q: A ray hits a plane mirror at 25 degrees to the mirror surface. Find the angle of incidence, the angle of reflection and the angle between the incident and reflected rays.
steps: The angle is given to the surface, so convert to the normal: angle of incidence = 90 - 25 = 65 degrees.
Law of reflection: angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 65 degrees.
Angle between the rays = angle of incidence + angle of reflection = 65 + 65 = 130 degrees.
worked.ans: i = 65 degrees, r = 65 degrees, angle between rays = 130 degrees.

worked.q: A ray enters a rectangular glass block with an angle of incidence of 50 degrees and is refracted at 30 degrees. State the angle of incidence inside the glass at the far (parallel) face and the angle at which the ray emerges into air.
steps: The two faces are parallel, so the normals are parallel.
The ray inside the glass meets the far face at the same angle it made with the first normal: 30 degrees.
Leaving the glass reverses the bending at entry, so the ray bends away from the normal to 50 degrees.
So the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.
worked.ans: Angle of incidence at far face = 30 degrees; emerges at 50 degrees, parallel to the incident ray.

worked.q: A student says a straw in a glass of water looks bent because the water bends the straw. Write a correct explanation.
steps: Light from the part of the straw under water travels from water into air.
At the water surface light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
The eye and brain trace the rays back in straight lines.
So the underwater part of the straw appears to be in a different, higher position.
worked.ans: The straw is not bent; refraction of light leaving the water makes the underwater part appear displaced, so the straw looks bent at the surface.

phy_ocra.13.3.summary: White light is a mixture of all the colours of the visible spectrum, each with a different wavelength and frequency. The colour we see an object as depends on **differential absorption, transmission and reflection**: which wavelengths it absorbs and which it reflects (opaque objects) or transmits (transparent and translucent objects). A red object looks red because it reflects red light and absorbs the rest; a red filter looks red because it transmits only red light. If the light shining on an object contains none of the colours it reflects, it appears black.

core.h: White light and the visible spectrum
core.p: **Visible light** is the small part of the electromagnetic spectrum our eyes can detect. **White light** is not a single colour but a **mixture of all the colours** of the visible spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. Each colour has its own **wavelength** and **frequency**.
bullets: **Red** light has the **longest wavelength** and **lowest frequency** in the visible spectrum.
**Violet** light has the **shortest wavelength** and **highest frequency**.
Visible wavelengths are roughly **400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red)**.
All colours travel at the **same speed** in a vacuum.
A prism splits white light into a spectrum because each colour refracts by a slightly different amount (dispersion).

callouts.p: A mixture of all the wavelengths (colours) of the visible spectrum.
Each colour of light corresponds to a particular range of wavelengths (and frequencies).

fig.cap: The visible spectrum. Red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency; violet has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency. White light contains all of these colours.

core.h: Three things light can do at a surface
core.p: When light meets an object, each wavelength can be **absorbed**, **transmitted** or **reflected**. The word **differential** means different wavelengths are treated differently: some are absorbed while others are reflected or transmitted. This is what gives objects their colour.
bullets: **Absorbed**: the light energy is taken in by the material (it warms up slightly); that colour is removed.
**Transmitted**: the light passes through the material.
**Reflected**: the light bounces off the surface.
The colour we see is made of the wavelengths that **reach our eyes**, i.e. those reflected or transmitted.
Most objects do a mixture of all three to different degrees for different wavelengths.

head: Process
What happens to the wavelength
Effect on what we see
rows: Energy taken in by the material
That colour seen through the object
That colour seen on the object

callouts.p: Different wavelengths of light are absorbed by different amounts by a material.

core.p: Materials are classified by how much light passes through them. This decides whether their colour comes mainly from reflection or from transmission.
bullets: **Opaque**: no light is transmitted; light is either reflected or absorbed. Colour comes from **reflection**.
**Transparent**: light is transmitted with little scattering, so you can see clearly through it (clear glass).
**Translucent**: light is transmitted but **scattered**, so you cannot see a clear image through it (frosted glass, tissue paper).
Coloured transparent and translucent objects get their colour from the wavelengths they **transmit**.

head: Material type
Light passes through?
Can you see a clear image through it?
Example

callouts.p: A material that does not transmit any light.
A material that transmits light but scatters it so no clear image is seen.

core.p: An opaque object appears the colour of the wavelengths it **reflects**. It **absorbs** all the other wavelengths. In white light a red apple reflects red light into your eyes and absorbs orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.
bullets: **Red object**: reflects red, absorbs all other colours.
**Green object**: reflects green, absorbs all other colours.
**White object**: reflects **all** wavelengths equally (absorbs none, ideally).
**Black object**: absorbs **all** wavelengths and reflects none.
Objects that reflect a mix of wavelengths appear a mixed colour, e.g. yellow can be red + green reflected together.

callouts.p: You see the colour that is reflected; every other colour is absorbed.

fig.cap: A red opaque object in white light. Only red wavelengths are reflected to the eye; all the other colours are absorbed, so the object appears red.

core.p: White and black are the two extreme cases of differential absorption. A **white** surface reflects all visible wavelengths, so all colours reach your eye and mix back into white. A **black** surface absorbs all visible wavelengths, so no light reaches your eye from it.
bullets: Black is **not a colour of light**; it is the **absence** of reflected light.
A white surface looks the colour of whatever light falls on it: white paper in red light looks red.
A black surface looks black in any colour of light.
Black objects absorb more energy, which is why dark clothes get hotter in the Sun.

callouts.p: Do not write that a black object reflects black light. It absorbs all wavelengths and reflects none.

core.p: An object can only reflect colours that are **in the light shining on it**. If the incident light contains none of the wavelengths the object normally reflects, the object reflects nothing and appears **black**.
bullets: Red object in **red light**: reflects the red, appears **red**.
Red object in **blue light**: absorbs the blue, reflects nothing, appears **black**.
White object in **green light**: reflects the green, appears **green**.
Green object in **red light**: absorbs the red, appears **black**.
Black object in any light: appears **black**.

callouts.p: Step 1: what colours are in the light hitting it? Step 2: which of those does the object reflect? If none, it looks black.

fig.cap: A red object lit only by blue light. The object absorbs the blue light and there is no red light to reflect, so nothing reaches the eye and it appears black.

core.p: A **colour filter** is a transparent coloured material. It **transmits** only its own colour and **absorbs** all others. Filters do not add colour to light; they **remove** colours from it.
bullets: **Red filter**: transmits red, absorbs all other colours.
White light through a red filter becomes **red light**.
Blue light through a red filter: blue absorbed, nothing transmitted, so **no light (black)**.
Two filters in a row: only colours transmitted by **both** get through; red then green filter lets **no light** through.
The brightness of transmitted light is **less** than the incident light because energy is absorbed.

callouts.p: A transparent material that transmits only certain wavelengths (its own colour) and absorbs the rest.
A red filter does not turn light red; it absorbs every colour except red.

core.p: Coloured glass, stained glass windows, coloured plastic and sweet wrappers behave like filters. They appear the colour they **transmit** when you look through them, because those wavelengths reach your eye and the rest are absorbed.
bullets: Green bottle glass transmits green and absorbs other colours.
Stained glass windows look bright from inside a church because sunlight is **transmitted** through them.
A coloured transparent object may also **reflect** some of its colour from its surface.
Looking at a red object through a green filter: red light from the object is absorbed by the filter, so the object looks **black**.

core.p: When a wavelength is absorbed, the **energy** carried by that light is transferred to the material, mostly increasing its internal (thermal) energy. Different materials (pigments and dyes) are able to absorb different wavelengths, which is why they have different colours.
bullets: Absorbed light energy usually **heats** the material slightly.
**Pigments** and **dyes** are chemicals that absorb particular wavelengths strongly.
This is why a dark car seat gets hotter in sunlight than a white one.
Plants look green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light strongly for photosynthesis and reflects green.

callouts.p: Absorbed light is not destroyed; its energy is transferred to the thermal store of the material.

core.h: Combining reflection and filters: worked logic
core.p: Harder questions combine coloured light, filters and coloured objects. Trace the light step by step from the source to the eye, removing colours at each stage.
bullets: Step 1: list the colours in the source light.
Step 2: remove any colours absorbed by a filter in front of the source.
Step 3: at the object, keep only the colours it reflects.
Step 4: if there is a filter in front of the eye, keep only colours it transmits.
Step 5: whatever remains is the colour seen; if nothing remains, the object appears **black**.

callouts.p: In the exam write: white light -> red filter -> red light -> blue object absorbs red -> no light reflected -> appears black. Each arrow is often a mark.

core.h: Wavelength, frequency and colour in exam answers
core.p: Mark schemes reward linking colour to **wavelength** (or frequency). Saying 'the object reflects red wavelengths of light' is better than 'it reflects red'.
bullets: Use the phrase **'reflects wavelengths corresponding to red light'**.
Use **'absorbs all other wavelengths'** for the remaining colours.
For filters: **'transmits'** not 'lets through' (though both are usually accepted).
Remember the spectrum order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (longest to shortest wavelength).

core.p: Differential absorption, transmission and reflection explain many everyday colour effects and are used in technology.
bullets: **Stage lighting**: coloured filters (gels) on spotlights change the colour of costumes on stage.
**Sunglasses and tinted windows** absorb some wavelengths to reduce glare.
**Clothes in shops**: colours can look different under shop lighting compared with daylight because the light contains different wavelengths.
**Traffic lights**: white bulbs behind red, amber and green filters (older designs).
**Photography filters** absorb unwanted wavelengths.

analogy.p: Think of an object as a bouncer and white light as a crowd of people wearing seven different coloured shirts. A red object's bouncer only lets red-shirted people bounce back out to you; everyone else is pulled inside (absorbed). A red filter is a bouncer on a doorway who only lets red shirts walk through to the other side. If only blue-shirted people turn up, the red bouncer sends nobody out, so the street stays empty: the object looks black. Where it breaks down: absorbed light does not stay inside as 'people', its energy is transferred to heating the material, and real objects rarely reflect only one perfectly pure colour.

mistakes.r: A red object reflects red light and absorbs all other colours.

mistakes.w: A red filter adds red colour to the light.
mistakes.r: A red filter transmits red and absorbs all other colours; it removes colours.

mistakes.w: A black object reflects black light.
mistakes.r: A black object absorbs all wavelengths and reflects none.

mistakes.w: A red object in blue light looks purple.
mistakes.r: It absorbs the blue and has no red light to reflect, so it appears black.

mistakes.w: A white object in red light still looks white.
mistakes.r: A white object reflects all colours present; only red is present, so it looks red.

mistakes.r: Red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency in the visible spectrum; violet the shortest.

exam.q: What is white light?
model: A mixture of all the colours / wavelengths of the visible spectrum.
exam.tip: Use the word mixture.

exam.q: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
model: Red.
exam.tip: Red longest wavelength, lowest frequency; violet the opposite.

exam.q: Explain why a leaf appears green in white light.
model: It reflects green light (wavelengths).
It absorbs all the other colours.
exam.tip: Two processes, two marks: reflect and absorb.

exam.q: State what is meant by an opaque material.
model: A material that does not transmit any light (light is reflected or absorbed).
exam.tip: Contrast with transparent and translucent.

exam.q: Explain why a white shirt appears blue when it is lit only by blue light.
model: A white object reflects all wavelengths that fall on it.
Only blue light falls on it, so only blue light is reflected to the eye.
exam.tip: Always check what colours are in the incident light.

exam.q: A red filter is placed in front of a white light source. Describe and explain what is seen on a white screen.
model: The screen appears red.
The filter transmits red light and absorbs all other colours; the white screen reflects the red light.
exam.tip: Mention transmit and absorb for the filter.

exam.q: A blue book is lit by red light. State and explain what colour it appears.
model: Black.
The book absorbs red light and there is no blue light to reflect, so no light reaches the eye.
exam.tip: Black means no light reflected, not a colour of light.

exam.q: Explain the difference between transparent and translucent materials, giving an example of each.
model: Transparent materials transmit light with little scattering.
So a clear image can be seen through them, e.g. clear glass.
Translucent materials transmit light but scatter it.
So no clear image is seen, e.g. frosted glass or tissue paper.
exam.tip: Give a correct example for each to secure all four marks.

exam.q: White light shines through a green filter onto a red apple. State and explain the colour the apple appears.
model: The green filter transmits only green light and absorbs other colours.
Only green light reaches the apple.
The red apple absorbs green light / only reflects red.
No light is reflected, so the apple appears black.
exam.tip: Follow the light from source to eye, removing colours at each stage.

exam.q: Explain how the colour of objects and filters is related to the differential absorption, transmission and reflection of different wavelengths of light. Use examples in your answer.
model: White light is a mixture of all visible wavelengths; each colour has a different wavelength.
Opaque objects reflect some wavelengths and absorb others; they appear the colour of the wavelengths reflected, e.g. a red object reflects red, absorbs others.
White objects reflect all wavelengths; black objects absorb all wavelengths.
Filters / transparent coloured objects transmit some wavelengths and absorb the rest, e.g. a red filter transmits only red.
An object lit by light containing none of the colours it reflects appears black, e.g. a red object in blue light.
Absorbed light energy is transferred to the material (heating it).
exam.tip: Cover reflection, transmission and absorption each with an example for full marks.

worked.q: A stage performer wears a white shirt, red trousers and a green hat. The stage is lit with red light only. What colour does each item appear?
steps: Only red light is present.
White shirt reflects all colours present, so it reflects red: appears red.
Red trousers reflect red: appear red.
Green hat reflects only green, but there is no green light; it absorbs red: appears black.
worked.ans: Shirt red, trousers red, hat black.

worked.q: White light passes through a blue filter and then a red filter. What reaches the screen?
steps: White light contains all colours.
The blue filter transmits only blue light and absorbs the rest.
The red filter absorbs blue light and only transmits red, but no red light reaches it.
No light passes through the second filter.
worked.ans: No light reaches the screen; it appears dark (black).

worked.q: A yellow banana is said to reflect red and green light. Predict its colour in red light, green light and blue light.
steps: In red light: the banana reflects red, so it appears red.
In green light: the banana reflects green, so it appears green.
In blue light: the banana absorbs blue and has no red or green to reflect, so it appears black.
worked.ans: Red in red light, green in green light, black in blue light.
